title: Character Creation Is a Program, Not a Form
description:
Tell the story of dependency-aware character creation.

Narrative hook and core question: Why not just ask the model to make a legal character?

Research initial model-generated character blobs, unsupported class or ancestry choices, impossible ability-score arrays, and the level-one HP maximum of -4. Explain why validating a complete object after generation is insufficient. Cover concept-first and ability-first creation modes, CharacterDraft, incremental dependency-aware validation, rules-pack-backed legal choice enumeration, required-choice descriptors, prerequisites, derived values, equipment and spell-choice workflows, save/resume, and how the same architecture informs level-up and progression.

Expected architectural conclusion: character creation is a stateful dependency graph disguised as a questionnaire.

Boundary: the existing rules-pack story uses character creation as evidence that prose is not enough. Cover the larger workflow and state-machine architecture without repeating the compiler story.

Use repository history, PRs, design docs, ADRs, audits, and playtest transcripts as evidence. Verify claims against artifacts rather than model memory; distinguish implemented behavior from planned architecture; preserve public readability and search indexing; and follow Joseph's voice rules: analytical and curious, concrete before abstraction, dry humor when earned, deliberate we/I attribution, reflect praise, absorb blame, no em dashes, and no generic LLM prose.
